Grammar
Infinitive Complements
Persuade + object + to-infinitive
Use when someone convinces another person to do something.
Her manager persuaded her to sign with a major label.
The video persuaded me to listen to her album.
Want + object + to-infinitive
Use to express a desire for someone else to do something.
I want you to hear this song.
She wanted her parents to watch her performance.
Believe + object + to-infinitive
Use when you think something is true about someone/something. (More formal than believe + that clause.)
Critics believe her to be the next big star.
I believe him to have real talent.
Make + object + base form (bare infinitive)
Important: After make, we do NOT use to. This is a bare infinitive.
The beat makes me want to dance.
His story made me cry.
Success made her work even harder.
Remember: Persuade, want, and believe are followed by to + infinitive. Make is followed by the base form (no to).

Compare: She wanted me to sing. vs. She made me sing.

Reading
Hip Hop Goes Home: A Struggling Rapper in Africa

🎤 Hip Hop Goes Home

Kofi Mensah left Accra, Ghana, when he was nineteen. Like thousands of young Africans before him, he dreamed of making it in New York City. He believed America to be the only place where a rapper could become a star. His parents wanted him to stay and study engineering, but Kofi persuaded them to let him try music for just one year.

That one year turned into eight long years of struggle. Kofi worked as a security guard at night and wrote rhymes during the day. He performed at small clubs in Brooklyn and the Bronx, but record labels rejected him again and again. "They said my accent was too strong," Kofi remembers. "They wanted me to sound like everyone else. But I didn't want to lose who I was."

Then, in 2019, everything changed. Kofi's mother called to tell him his grandfather was sick. She wanted Kofi to come home. The news made him book a flight immediately. He didn't know it then, but that trip would change his career forever.

Back in Accra, Kofi discovered something surprising. Hip hop was everywhere—in the markets, on the radio, in the clubs. But it sounded different. Local artists were mixing American-style rap with traditional Ghanaian highlife music, using drums and languages that Kofi had grown up with. "It made me realize I had been trying to run away from my own sound," he says.

Kofi decided to stay. He convinced a local producer to work with him, and together they created an album that blended New York hip-hop beats with Ghanaian folk melodies. The first single, "Accra to Brooklyn," became an overnight sensation. Within months, Kofi was performing at festivals across West Africa. Music critics believe him to be one of the most important voices in modern African hip hop.

Today, Kofi runs a small studio in Accra where he teaches young artists. He wants them to understand that they don't need to leave home to make it. "New York taught me discipline," he says. "But Ghana taught me who I am. The world doesn't need another copy. It needs your real voice."

Writing
A Profile of a Person You Admire
Writing Strategy — Paraphrasing: When you write a profile, you often need to include information from other sources. Paraphrasing means expressing someone else's ideas in your own words. Don't just copy. Change the vocabulary and sentence structure, but keep the same meaning.

Original vs. Paraphrase

Original: "Kofi left Ghana because he believed America was the only place where he could become a successful rapper."

Paraphrase: "Believing that the United States offered the only path to success in hip hop, Mensah moved from Ghana to New York."

Model Profile: Esmee Denters

Esmee Denters is a Dutch singer who became an overnight YouTube sensation in the late 2000s. Born in 1988 in the Netherlands, she began posting cover songs on YouTube while she was still a teenager. Her breakthrough came when pop star Justin Timberlake shared one of her videos, which persuaded millions of viewers to subscribe to her channel. Record labels soon wanted her to sign a contract, and in 2009 she became the first artist to join Timberlake's own label, Tennman Records. Although her early career faced challenges, Denters remained determined to accomplish her goals. Today, she continues to make music and inspire young artists who dream of turning online talent into real-world success.

Exercise B — Write your own profile

Choose a musician, artist, or performer you admire. Write a short profile (150-200 words). Use at least two examples of paraphrasing from research.

Structure: 1) Introduction (who, what, when) 2) Early life and career 3) Breakthrough moment 4) Why you admire them

Speaking
Analyzing a Music Contract
Speaking Strategy — Talking Pros and Cons: When you analyze a decision, it helps to list the advantages (pros) and disadvantages (cons). Use phrases like On the one hand... On the other hand... and The good thing is... The problem is...

📋 The Contract Offer

A record label has offered your band a five-year contract. Here are the terms:

📝 The label will pay for recording and touring costs.
📝 The band must produce at least two albums during the contract.
📝 The label keeps 60% of all profits; the band receives 40%.
📝 The band cannot record with any other label during this time.
📝 The label has the right to reject any songs they don't like.
✅ Pros (Advantages)
❌ Cons (Disadvantages)
Roleplay: Artist vs. Manager

Artist: You are unsure about the contract. Ask questions and express your concerns. Use "I want to know..." and "I believe this to be..."

Manager: You think the band should sign. Persuade the artist. Use "I want you to consider..." and "This deal will make us..."

Useful Phrases

Presenting pros: "The advantage is..." / "One good thing about this is..." / "On the positive side..."

Presenting cons: "The downside is..." / "One problem is..." / "On the other hand..."

Reaching a conclusion: "After weighing the pros and cons, I think..." / "All things considered..."

Expanding Your Fluency
Stage Fright or Stage Light?
Scenario Discussion

Work in groups of three. Each person receives a different role card. Use infinitive complements in your discussion.

Student A: The Nervous Performer

You have stage fright. You want your friends (help) you. You believe the audience (judge) you harshly. Persuade your teacher to let you record a video instead of performing live.

Student B: The Supportive Friend

You want your friend (face) their fear. You believe live performance (be) the best way to grow. Make them feel confident.

Student C: The Teacher

You want both students (find) a compromise. You believe a small classroom performance (build) confidence before a big stage. Persuade them to try a mini-concert first.
